paras.text: Flame photometer has both qualitative and quantitative applications. The radiations emitted by the flame photometer are characteristic to particular metal. Flame photometer with monochromators emits radiations of characteristic wavelengths which help to detect the presence of a particular metal in the sample. The concentration of unknown solution can be calculated from working curve of standard solutions. This technique is usually used to find the concentration of various alkali and alkaline earth metals in soil samples which are critical for soil cultivation. Flame photometry is also used to determine the concentrations of Na⁺ and K⁺ ions in biological samples and also estimation of various metals in soft drinks and juices.

paras.text: Atomic absorption spectrophotometry is used for the analysis of elements. The sample solution is evaporated in a flame, and the sample is converted to atomic vapour. Some of the atoms in the flame get excited but majority of them are in ground state. When light of particular wave length from the hollow cathode lamp is passed through these vapours atoms, they absorb the light for excitation from ground state to high energy state. The absorbance of light by atoms is directly proportional to the concentration of atomic vapours in the flame. For the analysis of different elements different types of lamps are used which produce light of different wave lengths. Each element shows absorption of particular wave length. Before introducing the sample of unknown concentration, solution of known concentrations of that element are aspirated into the flame one by one. Their absorbances are recorded and a working curve is constructed, between concentration and absorbance. Then sample of unknown concentration is aspirated into the flame and its concentration is determined from their absorbance using working curve.

The excited atoms loose energy of characteristic wavelength, which is dispersed by a grating or prism and detected in the spectrophotometer. The intensity of light emitted by the atoms is directly proportional to the concentration of analyte.

Flame photometer has both qualitative and quantitative applications. The radiations emitted by the flame photometer are characteristic to particular metal. Flame photometer with monochromators emits radiations of characteristic wavelengths which help to detect the presence of a particular metal in the sample. The concentration of unknown solution can be calculated from working curve of standard solutions. This technique is usually used to find the concentration of various alkali and alkaline earth metals in soil samples which are critical for soil cultivation. Flame photometry is also used to determine the concentrations of Na⁺ and K⁺ ions in biological samples and also estimation of various metals in soft drinks and juices.

Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry

Atomic absorption spectrophotometry is used for the analysis of elements. The sample solution is evaporated in a flame, and the sample is converted to atomic vapour. Some of the atoms in the flame get excited but majority of them are in ground state. When light of particular wave length from the hollow cathode lamp is passed through these vapours atoms, they absorb the light for excitation from ground state to high energy state. The absorbance of light by atoms is directly proportional to the concentration of atomic vapours in the flame. For the analysis of different elements different types of lamps are used which produce light of different wave lengths. Each element shows absorption of particular wave length. Before introducing the sample of unknown concentration, solution of known concentrations of that element are aspirated into the flame one by one. Their absorbances are recorded and a working curve is constructed, between concentration and absorbance. Then sample of unknown concentration is aspirated into the flame and its concentration is determined from their absorbance using working curve.

Atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for the estimation of over sixty metals in polluted water, body fluids, soft drinks etc.
